title: Seven Dead, Dozens Trapped as Landslide and Gas Leak Devastate Sikkim Tunnel
excerpt: A methane blast triggered a landslide that sealed an under-construction tunnel in Namchi district, trapping at least 27 workers as rescue teams battle toxic gas.
body:
• A landslide triggered by a suspected methane explosion sealed an under-construction tunnel in Sikkim's Namchi district on Monday, trapping at least 27 workers
  • The district administration confirmed seven fatalities as of Monday evening, with rescue operations slowed by a gas leak inside the tunnel
  • Several rescue workers reported dizziness and loss of consciousness from the toxic fumes, forcing teams to adopt cautious, phased approaches
  • The incident comes amid heavy monsoon rains across northeastern India, which have triggered landslides and flooding in multiple states

Methane Blast Triggers Deadly Collapse

A suspected methane explosion triggered a devastating landslide at an under-construction tunnel in Sikkim's Namchi district on Monday, killing at least seven workers and trapping approximately 27 others inside the sealed passage.

https://x.com/ShivAroor/status/2079392315085631953

The blast occurred during active construction work, sending a wall of rock and debris crashing across the tunnel entrance and cutting off workers deep inside. India Today reported that the methane blast preceded the landslide, creating a lethal chain of events that left rescue teams facing both structural instability and toxic gas exposure.

By Monday evening, the Namchi district administration had confirmed seven fatalities, according to ANI News, though the exact number of workers still trapped remained fluid as officials worked to reconcile multiple headcounts from contractors.

"In neighbouring Jammu and Kashmir, a landslide in Poonch district's Loran village killed seven people, including four women, after a mud house collapsed."

Gas Leak Slows Rescue Effort

The rescue operation has been severely hampered by a suspected gas leak inside the tunnel. Multiple rescue workers reported feeling dizzy upon entering the passage, and several lost consciousness, according to officials at the site.

The National Disaster Response Force and state disaster management teams were deployed to the site, but the gas hazard forced them to adopt a cautious, phased approach rather than the rapid entry operation families of the trapped workers were hoping for.

"There is a suspected gas leak inside the tunnel, making rescue operations difficult. Some workers involved in the rescue effort reportedly felt dizzy, while a few lost consciousness."

— District administration officials, per reports

Authorities have requested specialised gas detection and ventilation equipment from the Indian Army and NDRF. Communication with the trapped workers has been intermittent, with officials unable to confirm how many of those inside are injured.

Monsoon Compounds the Crisis

The tunnel collapse is the latest in a series of monsoon-triggered disasters across India's northeast. In neighbouring Jammu and Kashmir, a landslide in Poonch district's Loran village killed seven people, including four women, after a mud house collapsed. Assam continues to reel from flooding that has claimed five lives and affected more than 57,100 people, with the Indian Army deployed for relief operations.

ISRO satellite imagery showed monsoon clouds covering nearly 70 percent of India on Monday, with heavy rainfall expected across northern, eastern, and northeastern regions through July 25. The India Meteorological Department has issued red alerts for heavy rain in Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh.

Infrastructure Safety Under Scrutiny

The Sikkim tunnel disaster is likely to reignite questions about construction safety standards in India's ambitious infrastructure push across the Himalayan region. The 2023 Uttarakhand tunnel collapse, which trapped 41 workers for 17 days before a dramatic rescue, exposed systemic gaps in safety protocols for high-altitude construction projects.

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom hail from northeastern states, the disaster underscores the human cost of rapid infrastructure development in geologically fragile terrain. Environmental groups have repeatedly warned that large-scale construction in the Himalayas increases the risk of landslides and tunnel failures, particularly during the monsoon season.

Rescue operations are expected to continue through the night. Officials have urged families gathering at the site to remain patient as teams work to ventilate the tunnel and establish safe entry points.
